findings.title: `dbp` holds impossible values and unusual ones, and they are different categories.
findings.detail: 4 values in `dbp` are outside 10–200 mmHg, limits no living adult is expected to show (a convention: CLINICAL_SURVEY_PACK §A1.2's suggested EHR-cleaning bounds). 4 of `dbp`'s values are 0. NHANES records a diastolic pressure of 0 on purpose (NHANES 2017-2018 BPX_J documentation, Data Processing and Editing: 'Diastolic BP can be zero'; BPXDI1 range of values 0 to 136.): it is a reading, not an entry error, and it is conventionally set to missing. This is different from the 26 adult values outside 42–100 mmHg, the central 98% of adults aged 20 and over in NHANES 2017-2018 (weighted 1st and 99th percentiles, BPXDI1): unusual but real, and they must be kept, because excluding them would remove the sickest patients. The same reading applies to `height_cm`, `sbp`, `glucose`, `weight_kg`.
findings.why_it_matters: Physiologically impossible and statistically extreme are different categories, and no generic outlier rule can tell them apart. The impossible values are a data-quality repair with a count that belongs in the paper; the unusual ones are the case mix the model exists to learn. Every limit here is a convention, with its source.

evidence.source: research/CLINICAL_SURVEY_PACK.md#A1.2 ★ Reference ranges vs physiological plausibility — the distinction that matters
